Here's how to drop the frontend into your VS Code project:

1. Save the file

In VS Code, create a new file in your project folder:
plain
Copy
your-project/
├── backend.py          ← your existing backend
├── index.html          ← the new frontend (save it here)
└── ...
To save: Press Ctrl+S (or Cmd+S on Mac) and name it index.html in the same folder as your backend.

2. Point it to your backend

Open index.html and find this line near the top of the <script> section:
JavaScript
Copy
const API_BASE = "http://localhost:8000";   // ← change this if your backend uses a different port
Update it to match wherever your backend runs (e.g., http://localhost:5000, http://127.0.0.1:8080, etc.).

3. Run it

Option A — VS Code Live Server (easiest):
  • Install the "Live Server" extension by Ritwick Dey
  • Right-click index.html → "Open with Live Server"
  • It opens in your browser automatically
Option B — Python (if you already have it running for backend):
bash
Copy
# In a new terminal, from your project folder:
python -m http.server 3000
# Then open http://localhost:3000
Option C — Just double-click: Open index.html directly in your browser. This works fine, but if your backend and frontend are on different ports, you'll need CORS enabled on your backend (which your FastAPI backend already has).

4. Test the connection

  1. Start your backend first
  2. Open the frontend
  3. Fill in the form and hit Run Analysis
  4. Check your browser's DevTools (F12 → Network tab) to see if the request hits your backend
If you get a CORS error, make sure your backend has this middleware (your FastAPI file already does):
Python
Copy
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware, allow_origins=["*"], ...)
That's it — the frontend is a single file you can edit directly in VS Code.

I see — your main.py is a terminal CLI tool, not a web API. It reads input from the keyboard and prints to the terminal. The frontend I built expects a web API (HTTP requests/JSON responses).
You have two options:

Option 1: Wrap your CLI in a FastAPI backend (recommended)

Keep your existing logic but expose it as a web API. Here's a minimal wrapper you can add to your project:
Create api.py in the same folder as main.py:
Python
Copy
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional
import subprocess
import json
import re

app = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

class AnalyzeRequest(BaseModel):
    country: str
    product_category: str
    sector: Optional[str] = ""
    date_range: Optional[str] = "auto"

@app.post("/api/analyze")
def analyze(req: AnalyzeRequest):
    # Run your CLI tool and feed it inputs
    proc = subprocess.Popen(
        ["python", "main.py"],
        stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
        text=True
    )
    
    # Feed the inputs your CLI expects
    inputs = f"{req.country}\n{req.product_category}\n{req.sector or ''}\n{req.date_range or 'auto'}\n"
    stdout, stderr = proc.communicate(input=inputs, timeout=30)
    
    # Parse the terminal output into JSON
    # (You'll need to adjust this based on what main.py actually prints)
    return {
        "raw_output": stdout,
        "query": {
            "country": req.country,
            "product_category": req.product_category,
            "sector": req.sector,
            "date_range": req.date_range
        }
    }

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)
Then run:
bash
Copy
python api.py
And the frontend will connect to http://localhost:8000.

Option 2: Convert your CLI logic directly to FastAPI

If you can share your main.py (or paste it here), I can convert it into a proper FastAPI backend that the frontend can talk to. This is cleaner than wrapping a CLI.

Option 3: Keep it as a CLI, skip the web frontend

If you just want a nicer terminal experience, that's different from a web app.
Which option do you want? If you paste your main.py code, I can convert it to a proper API in about 2 minutes.

Yes — your pipeline hits the Federal Register API, downloads PDFs, extracts text, then runs Ollama (Mistral) locally for each EO. That's a lot of work per request.
Here are ways to speed it up:

1. Use cached data (already built in)

Your cache_manager.py caches EOs for 1 day. If you already ran an analysis today, it skips the Federal Register fetch. But the Ollama calls still happen every time — that's the slow part.

2. Skip Ollama for a faster demo

I can add a "fast mode" endpoint that skips the AI analysis and just uses the regex pre-filter results. It won't be as smart, but it'll load in seconds instead of minutes.
Want me to add a ?fast=true query parameter to your api.py?

3. Pre-run the full pipeline once

Run your CLI tool once to populate the cache, then the API will reuse it:
bash
Copy
cd /Users/derek/Desktop/EO-Analyzer
python main.py
# Enter: China, semiconductors, (blank), auto
This fills eo_cache.json. Then your API won't re-fetch from Federal Register.

4. Check if Ollama is the bottleneck

In your api.py terminal, is it stuck on:
  • "Fetching executive orders..." → Federal Register is slow
  • "Analyzing with Ollama..." → Mistral is slow (normal, it's local AI)

What do you want?
  • A) Fast mode API (skips Ollama, uses regex only)
  • B) Just use the mock data for now (frontend works instantly)
  • C) Wait it out — your real pipeline is working, just slow

Here's a README for your project:

EO Import Impact Analyzer

A web application that analyzes US Executive Orders to identify impacts on costs and employment for import businesses. It fetches real Executive Orders from the Federal Register, filters them for trade relevance, and uses AI (local Ollama/Mistral) to extract structured tariff and impact data.

What It Does

Enter your import details — country, product category, sector, and date range — and the tool will:
  1. Fetch Executive Orders from the Federal Register API for your date range
  2. Filter them for trade/tariff relevance using regex patterns
  3. Pre-filter with smart regex to identify obviously relevant vs. ambiguous orders
  4. Analyze ambiguous orders with local AI (Ollama/Mistral) for relevance and impact
  5. Extract structured data: tariff mechanisms, HTS codes, effective dates, cost impacts, employment impacts
  6. Display everything in a sleek dark-mode dashboard with risk scores, charts, and recommendations

Architecture

Table
Copy
ComponentFilePurpose
Frontendindex.htmlDark-mode web UI with toggle switch for Fast/Full AI mode
APIapi.pyFastAPI backend that orchestrates the pipeline
Fetcherfed_register_fetcher.pyPulls EOs from Federal Register API + PDF text extraction
Filtertrade_filter.pyRegex-based trade/tariff keyword filtering
Pre-filtersmart_prefilter.pyClassifies EOs as obvious yes/no/ambiguous
AI Analyzerollama_analyzer.pyOllama/Mistral relevance and impact analysis
Impact Extractorimpact_extractor.pyStructured JSON extraction from EO text
Cachecache_manager.pyCaches Federal Register data for 1 day
CLImain.pyOriginal terminal interface (still works)

Quick Start

Prerequisites

  • Python 3.11+
  • Ollama installed with mistral model pulled
  • pip install fastapi uvicorn requests pdfplumber pycountry

1. Start Ollama

bash
Copy
ollama serve

2. Start the Backend

In a new terminal:
bash
Copy
cd /path/to/EO-Analyzer
python api.py
Backend runs at http://localhost:8000

3. Start the Frontend

In another new terminal:
bash
Copy
cd /path/to/EO-Analyzer
python -m http.server 3000
Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser.

Usage

  1. Enter your import details:
    • Country you're importing FROM (e.g., China, Vietnam, Mexico)
    • Product category (e.g., semiconductors, textiles, steel)
    • Optional sector/industry
    • Date range (auto = last 6 months)
  2. Choose Analysis Mode:
    • ⚡ Fast Mode (default): Uses regex pre-filter only. Results in ~5-10 seconds. Good for quick scans.
    • 🧠 Full AI Mode: Runs Ollama/Mistral analysis on each ambiguous EO. Results in ~2-5 minutes. More thorough and accurate.
  3. Click "Run Analysis"
  4. Review the dashboard:
    • Risk score (0-100)
    • Relevant Executive Orders with tariff rates and descriptions
    • Cost impact projections with before/after comparisons
    • Employment impact modeling
    • Strategic recommendations

Fast Mode vs. Full AI Mode

Table
Copy
Fast ModeFull AI Mode
Speed~5-10 seconds~2-5 minutes
MethodRegex pre-filter onlyOllama/Mistral AI analysis
AccuracyGood for obvious casesBetter for nuanced/ambiguous EOs
Use caseQuick scans, frequent checksDeep analysis, critical decisions

API Endpoints

Table
Copy
EndpointMethodDescription
/GETHealth check
/api/analyzePOSTMain analysis endpoint
/api/healthGETService health
POST /api/analyze body:
JSON
Copy
{
  "country": "China",
  "product_category": "semiconductors",
  "sector": "automotive",
  "date_range": "auto",
  "fast_mode": true
}

Data Sources

  • Federal Register API (federalregister.gov) — official source for all Presidential documents
  • Ollama (ollama.com) — local LLM inference using Mistral model

Files

plain
Copy
EO-Analyzer/
├── index.html              # Frontend web app
├── api.py                  # FastAPI backend
├── main.py                 # Original CLI tool
├── fed_register_fetcher.py # Federal Register API client
├── trade_filter.py         # Trade keyword filter
├── smart_prefilter.py      # Regex pre-classifier
├── ollama_analyzer.py      # AI relevance analyzer
├── impact_extractor.py     # Structured data extractor
├── cache_manager.py        # JSON cache manager
├── user_input.py           # CLI input handler
├── output_formatter.py     # CLI output formatter
└── eo_cache.json           # Local cache file

Notes

  • The Federal Register API is rate-limited. The tool includes 1-second delays between requests.
  • PDF text extraction uses pdfplumber — some complex PDF layouts may not extract perfectly.
  • Ollama must be running before starting the backend. The tool will retry connections up to 5 times.
  • Cache expires after 1 day. Delete eo_cache.json to force a fresh fetch.

A README on GitHub is just a text file. It doesn't need to be code — it's written in Markdown (a simple formatting language), but plain text works too.
When you upload README.md to GitHub, it automatically renders it as a nice formatted page below your code files.
Here's how to make one for your project:
In VS Code:
  1. Create a new file named README.md (the .md extension tells GitHub it's Markdown)
  2. Paste the text I wrote above
  3. Save it
  4. Commit and push to GitHub
GitHub will automatically display it on your repo's main page.
If you want, I can save the README as a proper .md file you can download:
Execute Python code
Here's your README.md file.
How to use it:
  1. Save it as README.md in your EO-Analyzer folder (same folder as main.py, api.py, etc.)
  2. Commit and push it to GitHub:
bash
Copy
cd /Users/derek/Desktop/EO-Analyzer
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git push
  1. Go to your GitHub repo page — the README will show up automatically as a formatted page below your files
What Markdown does: The # symbols make headings, --- makes dividers, | makes tables, and ``` makes code blocks. GitHub renders all of that nicely. You can write it in plain text too, but Markdown looks way better.

Your local branch is behind the remote. Run this:
bash
Copy
git pull origin main --rebase
git push
The --rebase puts your local commits on top of the remote ones, avoiding merge commits. If there are conflicts, it'll tell you which files to fix. After fixing them:
bash
Copy
git add .
git rebase --continue
git push
If you don't care about the remote changes and just want to overwrite them:
bash
Copy
git push -f origin main
But --rebase first is the cleaner approach.
